title: Michael Spence and the Economics of Job-Market Signaling (1973)
explainer: Economist Michael Spence showed, in a landmark 1973 paper, that credentials such as degrees can have real value to an employer even when the credential itself does not improve job performance, because what matters is that it is harder for a less-qualified candidate to obtain, so holding it still reliably signals ability. This work, part of what later won him a share of the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economics, is the formal underpinning of why resumes, portfolios, and certifications function as filters in hiring. It reframes job-search strategy as managing which credible signals you can send, not only which skills you actually have.
